title: Remove Letter To Equalize Frequency
spaceBreakdown:
- int freq[26]: fixed 26 ints → O(1)
- int fc[101]: fixed 101 ints → O(1)
- scalar locals (cnt, f1, c1, f2, c2): O(1)
- not counted: input string, returned bool
approach: Count how many times each of the 26 letters appears, then build a frequency-of-frequencies map (how many letters share each count value). The answer is true only in a few cases: (1) there is one distinct frequency and it is 1 (delete any letter) or only one distinct letter exists (delete one copy); (2) there are two distinct frequencies f1 < f2 where either f2 = f1+1 and exactly one letter has frequency f2 (delete one from it), or f1 = 1 and exactly one letter has frequency 1 (delete that lone letter). Any other configuration is impossible to fix with one deletion.
hints: If you list how many times each distinct letter appears, what is the largest number of different count values that list can contain while still being fixable by deleting a single character - and what must be special about those values?
Use a frequency array of size 26 for letters, then a second frequency-of-frequencies array. For "abcc", the letter counts are a:1, b:1, c:2, giving frequency-of-frequencies {1→2, 2→1}.

**Single distinct character** - all letters identical, only one frequency entry with count 1.
`Input: "zzz"` → `Expected: true`
⚠️ Bug: only checking the two-frequency case, never handling the single-frequency case where c==1 → returns false

**All frequencies are 1** - every letter appears exactly once.
`Input: "abc"` → `Expected: true`
⚠️ Bug: in the single-frequency case, requiring f > 1 before returning true → returns false

**Two equal frequencies, no outlier** - two letters each appear the same number of times greater than 1.
`Input: "aazz"` → `Expected: false`
⚠️ Bug: returning true whenever there is exactly one distinct frequency → returns true

**Lone frequency-1 letter** - one letter appears once, all others share a higher frequency.
`Input: "abbcc"` → `Expected: true`
⚠️ Bug: only checking the f2==f1+1 branch, ignoring the f1==1 branch → returns false

followUps.q: If word.length can be up to 10^5, does the approach change?
followUps.a: No. Counting is O(n) and the case analysis is O(26 + max_freq), both fine. The only adjustment is sizing the frequency-of-frequencies structure for max_freq up to 10^5 (use a hash map or a vector sized to n). Time stays O(n), space stays O(1) since at most 26 distinct letters exist.

followUps.q: What if you could remove up to k characters instead of exactly one?
followUps.a: This is harder: you must decide whether some target frequency t lets every letter reach t by removing between 0 and k total characters. A feasible approach iterates candidate target frequencies and sums the needed removals, giving O(26 · max_freq) time and O(1) space, but the greedy validity per target must be checked carefully.

followUps.q: What if the alphabet were Unicode with up to 10^6 distinct symbols?
followUps.a: Replace the size-26 array with a hash map for letter frequencies. The frequency-of-frequencies map then holds at most n entries. Time remains O(n); space becomes O(n) in the worst case when all symbols are distinct.
